name: Saffron
poem: The world's most expensive spice ground into a paint — three crocus stigmas per flower, seventy-five thousand flowers per pound, every harvest done by hand.

recipe.note: A warm orange-yellow, like late-afternoon light.

lenses.label: Art History
lenses.intro: Saffron's painters knew they were grinding the spice of kings — and the colour repaid them with a yellow no other dye-pigment could quite match.

entries.title: Persian Miniatures
entries.blurb: The exact gold of Persian palace domes and Sufi haloes is saffron tincture applied over gold leaf — a colour that doubles as a small fortune spent on each illustration.

entries.title: Illuminated Manuscripts
entries.blurb: Saffron yellow was used by monks as a cheap substitute for gold leaf in illuminated capitals — when the abbey couldn't afford bullion, the kitchen lent its spice.

entries.title: Saffron in Renaissance Frescoes
entries.blurb: The yellow robes of angels and prophets in Giotto's Padua frescoes — and many other church cycles — are largely saffron, glazed thin over pale undercoats.

lenses.label: Fashion
lenses.intro: Saffron-dyed cloth is the most expensive textile per gram in human history — a colour worn by people the rest of society needed to recognise instantly.

entries.title: Buddhist Monks' Robes
entries.blurb: Real saffron is too expensive for monastic dye — modern robes use turmeric or jackfruit wood. But the colour-name has carried forward for 2,500 years.

entries.title: Irish Léinte
entries.blurb: The saffron-dyed linen tunic was the badge of high Gaelic society — banned by the English in 1366 as a marker of "Irish wildness," a fashion law that lasted 250 years.

entries.title: Sikh Wedding Turbans
entries.blurb: Sikh grooms wear a kesari (saffron) turban for the wedding ceremony — the colour signals both sacred commitment and willingness to defend the bride for life.

lenses.label: Nature
lenses.intro: Saffron's source is one of the most agriculturally improbable success stories in history — a sterile autumn crocus that exists only because humans propagate it.

entries.title: Crocus sativus
entries.blurb: The saffron crocus is a triploid hybrid — sterile, unable to set seed, propagated only by dividing its corms. Every plant alive today descends from a single original.

entries.title: Hand-Picked Stigmas
entries.blurb: Each flower contains three red stigmas. They open at dawn and wilt within hours — every gram of saffron is the morning's labour of hundreds of hands.

entries.title: Late-Afternoon Sunlight
entries.blurb: The exact warm gold of saffron is the colour of sun at five o'clock in October — a colour Mediterranean cultures have spent millennia trying to bottle.

lenses.label: Pop Culture
lenses.intro: Saffron's status as the world's most expensive spice has made it shorthand for luxury in modern food culture — and a frequent target of adulteration.

entries.title: Spanish Paella
entries.blurb: The signature yellow of paella valenciana is genuine saffron — and the absence of it is the leading marker of a tourist trap. Real paella turns yellow halfway through cooking.

entries.title: The Saffron Revolution
entries.blurb: Buddhist monks led mass protests against the military junta, draped in their saffron robes — the colour gave the uprising its name, then its martyrs.

entries.title: Adulterated Saffron
entries.blurb: Saffron is among the most-faked foods in the world — cut with safflower, marigold, even dyed corn silk. Detection requires lab tests; price alone isn't a clue.

lenses.label: Etymology
lenses.intro: Saffron's name has crossed every major trade language and stayed remarkably consistent — when you're worth more than gold, your name travels intact.

entries.title: "Za'farān"
entries.blurb: The Arabic source of "saffron" — and probably of every European cognate. The word arrived in Spain with the Moors and spread north along the spice routes.

entries.title: "Krokos"
entries.blurb: The Greek name for the flower, from a much older Mediterranean root — Pliny notes saffron's use as both spice and dye in Phoenician records before the Greeks took it on.

entries.title: "Saffron Walden"
entries.blurb: An English market town named for its saffron fields — and home to a 14th-century industry rivalling Persia, before climate change and undercutting destroyed it.

lenses.label: Symbolism
lenses.intro: Saffron is one of the rare colours that carries the same broad meaning across every culture it touches — sacred, costly, joyful.

entries.title: Sacred Saffron
entries.blurb: The colour of the sun, the colour of renunciation, the colour of every flame in every temple lamp — saffron is the spiritual colour of South and Southeast Asia.

entries.title: The Indian Flag
entries.blurb: The top stripe of the tricolour is saffron — chosen to represent courage and sacrifice, and to honour the Hindu/Sikh/Buddhist traditions of the new republic.

entries.title: Wealth in Spice
entries.blurb: From Roman banquets to Tudor confectionery, serving saffron-dyed food was a public display of wealth — a kind of edible jewellery that signalled the host's reach.
